children.text: Discover the fundamental principles used to describe the motion of objects in space.

This course bridges theory and practice in astrodynamics. You will learn how to model, simulate and analyze the motion of spacecraft and satellites in realistic environments, account for uncertainties, assess conjunction risks and apply these skills to mission design and operations. Through interactive lectures, hands-on computations and case studies, you will develop the analytical and programming skills required to tackle real challenges in spaceflight, navigation and space domain awareness.

Model perturbations and assess their impact
Analyze relative motion and rendezvous dynamics
Propagate covariance and compute collision probability
Work with real catalogs of space debris and background stars
Apply astrodynamics to remote sensing mission analysis
Advanced concepts explained with clarity
Extensive hands-on exercises and projects
Real-world datasets and professional toolkits
Industry-relevant workflows and case studies
At the end...
Certificate of completion for your achievement
From equations to orbits, from models to missions

Develop the analytical rigor of a scientist, the practical mindset of an engineer, and the computational skills required to solve the astrodynamics challenges of the modern space age. Transform mathematical theory into operational capability through a program designed by a scientist, engineer, educator, and practitioner with experience spanning three decades in academia, industry, defence, and the international space community.

Modern space missions depend on professionals who can transform the mathematics of celestial mechanics into operational decisions. From orbit determination and mission design to conjunction assessment, collision avoidance, and Space Situational Awareness (SSA) / Space Domain Awareness (SDA), the demand for engineers and scientists trained in advanced astrodynamics has never been greater.

This professional training program bridges the gap between theory and practice by combining rigorous physical foundations with hands-on computational implementation using MATLAB/Octave, and Python. Participants learn not only the “why” behind orbital dynamics, but also the “how” used daily by flight dynamics engineers, mission analysts, SSA specialists, and spacecraft operators supporting real missions.

Designed for aerospace engineers, researchers, graduate students, and space professionals, the course progresses from classical orbital mechanics to contemporary topics including perturbation theory, numerical orbit propagation, orbit determination, relative motion, conjunction analysis, collision probability estimation, space debris modeling, and remote sensing mission applications.

Unlike traditional courses that stop at deriving equations, this program emphasizes implementation. Every major concept is reinforced through realistic case studies, numerical simulations, and scientific programming exercises. Participants build working computational tools while developing the physical intuition needed to understand and validate their results.

This program is created to complement—not replace—professional astrodynamics platforms such as Systems Tool Kit (STK). Participants will develop a deep understanding of the underlying orbital mechanics, perturbation models, estimation techniques, and numerical algorithms that power these tools, enabling them to use commercial software with greater confidence, rigor, and technical judgment.

There is no shortage of astrodynamics textbooks. What is rare is a course that teaches participants how to transform theory into operational capability. Most courses focus on equations. Most online programs focus on software tools. This course teaches both.

Every major concept is derived from first principles, implemented in code, validated against realistic scenarios, and connected directly to the workflows used by mission analysts, spacecraft operators, and Space Domain Awareness teams. Participants do not simply learn orbital mechanics—they learn how modern astrodynamics is actually practiced.
Learn by Building

Every topic is accompanied by executable MATLAB, Octave, and Python examples. Participants implement orbit propagators, perturbation models, conjunction assessment algorithms, covariance propagation methods, and collision probability calculations rather than treating them as black boxes.
Real Operational Workflows
The curriculum reflects the analytical processes used throughout the space industry:
Orbit propagation and mission analysis

From University Classroom to Industry Practice

Developed from advanced astrodynamics courses taught at Laval University and adapted for professional audiences, including presentation as a technical short course at the AMOS Conference, the premier international conference dedicated to Space Situational Awareness.
Understand Why, Not Just How

Participants learn the physical and mathematical foundations behind every model, algorithm, and numerical method. This enables them to design, evaluate, troubleshoot, and improve the computational tools used in operational environments.
Immediate Professional Relevance

The techniques covered are directly applicable to organizations involved in spacecraft operations, mission analysis, space surveillance, Earth observation, defense applications, and advanced aerospace research.
The result

Graduates leave with more than theoretical knowledge. They leave with a practical toolkit, working software implementations, and the confidence to really understand and tackle the astrodynamics challenges of modern space operations.

sections.title: WHY LEARNING ASTRODYNAMICS FROM PROFESSIONAL SOFTWARE IS SO DIFFICULT

children.text: Professional astrodynamics software is extremely powerful, but it is designed primarily to solve operational problems—not to teach the physics behind them.

Complex calculations are often performed behind the interface, making it difficult to see how orbital mechanics, perturbation models, reference frames, numerical methods, and estimation techniques actually work together.
Without this foundation, it can be challenging to understand why a model was selected, recognize when an assumption is no longer valid, or determine whether a result is physically meaningful.

This program takes the opposite approach: understand the physics first, implement the methods yourself, and then use professional software with greater confidence, technical judgment, and understanding.

sections.title: "A PICTURE IS WORTH A THOUSAND WORDS"

children.text: Orbital mechanics becomes much easier to understand when equations can be seen in action. Interactive simulations transform abstract mathematical concepts into trajectories, geometries, and motions that can be explored visually.
By changing orbital parameters and immediately observing their effects, you can develop an intuitive understanding of concepts that are often difficult to grasp from equations alone.
Throughout the program, visualization and simulation are used alongside theory to connect mathematical models with the physical behavior of real orbital systems.
Explore four progressive courses covering celestial mechanics, astrodynamics, space situational awareness, and remote sensing from space.

sections.title: Basic Astronomy and Celestial Mechanics

children.text: Students will study the structure of the Solar System, Newton’s laws, universal gravitation, Kepler’s laws, and the classical two-body problem.
Course Objective
By the end of this course, students will be able to explain the motion of celestial bodies using the fundamental laws of mechanics and gravitation.
Main Topics
Structure and scale of the Solar System
Celestial coordinate systems
Newton’s laws and universal gravitation
Kepler’s laws of planetary motion
The classical two-body problem
Energy and angular momentum
Key Question
How do the laws of mechanics explain the motion of planets and satellites?

sections.summary: This first course introduces the astronomical, physical, and mathematical foundations required to understand the motion of celestial bodies.

sections.title: Foundations of Astrodynamics

children.text: Students will learn to work with state vectors, reference frames, classical orbital elements, Keplerian propagation, and basic orbital maneuvers.
Course Objective
By the end of this course, students will be able to characterize an orbit, interpret its classical elements, and perform introductory trajectory calculations.
Main Topics
Position and velocity state vectors
Orbital reference frames and time systems
Classical orbital elements
Circular, elliptical, and escape trajectories
Keplerian orbit propagation
Introduction to orbital maneuvers
Key Question
How can a satellite’s position and velocity be used to predict its future trajectory?

sections.summary: The second course introduces the tools used to describe, calculate, and predict the trajectory of an artificial satellite or spacecraft.

sections.title: Applied Astrodynamics and Space Situational Awareness

children.text: Students will also discover the principles of Space Situational Awareness, including satellite tracking, orbit prediction, conjunction analysis, and the monitoring of space debris.
Course Objective
By the end of this course, students will be able to analyze perturbed trajectories, apply numerical propagation methods, and explain how orbital data supports safe operations in space.
Main Topics
Earth oblateness and the J2 perturbation
Atmospheric drag and solar radiation pressure
Third-body gravitational effects
Numerical orbit propagation
Satellite tracking and orbit determination
Conjunction analysis and space debris monitoring
Key Question
How can we predict and monitor satellite trajectories in a perturbed orbital environment?

sections.summary: This third course extends the two-body model by introducing the perturbations and numerical methods required to analyze real satellite trajectories.

sections.title: Remote Sensing from Space: Orbit-to-Image Physics

children.text: Students will examine how orbital altitude, viewing geometry, sensor characteristics, and radiometric conditions influence image coverage, spatial resolution, and revisit time.
Course Objective
By the end of this course, students will be able to relate an orbital configuration and sensor design to the geometry and quality of a remotely sensed image.
Main Topics
Principles of satellite remote sensing
Observation geometry and line of sight
Ground sampling distance and spatial resolution
Swath width, coverage, and revisit time
Radiometric and spectral considerations
From orbital position to image geolocation
Key Question
How do the orbit and sensor characteristics determine what can be observed in a satellite image?

sections.summary: The fourth course connects satellite orbit design with the physical principles of Earth observation and image acquisition from space.
